title: Public Goods
objective: After this level you can explain why things like roads and lighthouses are usually paid for by governments.
summary: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, so people can free ride and markets underprovide them. Taxes fix that. Coase found England's lighthouses were paid for by port dues.

cards.headline: Economists' go-to example for a century: the lighthouse. Then someone checked.
cards.body: From John Stuart Mill to Paul Samuelson, the lighthouse stood for something markets supposedly couldn't provide: how would you make a passing ship pay for the light? To see the problem, start with a fireworks show.

cards.headline: The fireworks problem
cards.body: Someone has to pay for the town's fireworks show. But once the rockets go up, anyone can watch from their own backyard. So each person has a reason to let others pay and enjoy the show for free. Economists call that free riding. If enough people do it, the money never comes in, and a show everyone would have enjoyed simply never happens.

cards.headline: Public goods
cards.body: Fireworks are a public good, with two features. They're nonexcludable: it's costly or impossible to stop non-payers from enjoying them. And they're nonrival: your watching doesn't use up anyone else's view. National defense is the classic case, protecting everyone in a country at once. The usual fix is the one from Level 51: people agree through politics to pay taxes for it, and the free riders have nowhere to hide.

cards.fact: England's early lighthouses were often privately run, paid for by fees collected at ports.
cards.context: In 1974, economist Ronald Coase dug into the history. Ships that passed a light still had to dock somewhere, and there they paid light dues. Free riding solved? Critics point out that the right to collect those dues came from a royal patent, so government was still doing the enforcing. The lighthouse turned out to be a debate, not a textbook certainty.

cards.headline: Public goods: explained
learned: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival
Coase's lighthouses were paid for at the port

questions.prompt: Which two features make something a public good?

options.label: It is expensive and rare
options.rationale: Public goods are defined by who can use them, not by price.

options.label: Non-payers cannot easily be excluded, and one person using it does not use it up
It is sold in shops and taxed at the till
options.rationale: That describes ordinary goods with a sales tax.

options.label: It is made by the government and given away
options.rationale: Who makes it is not the test: Coase found private lighthouses.

questions.explanation: A public good is nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense.

questions.prompt: Why might a fireworks show paid for by voluntary donations never happen?

options.label: Fireworks are banned in most towns
options.rationale: The problem is about paying, not permission.

options.label: Only a few people enjoy fireworks
options.rationale: The show would be enjoyed by many; that is the point.

options.label: People can watch for free, so many let others pay
The show gets worse as more people watch
options.rationale: It's nonrival: extra watchers don't spoil it.

questions.explanation: When non-payers cannot be kept out, people free ride, and too little money comes in.

questions.prompt: How did the light dues Coase studied get around free riding?

options.label: Ships were charged when they docked, so users of the light could be made to pay
Lighthouse keepers switched the light off for ships that had not paid
options.rationale: The light shone for everyone; the charge came at the port.

options.label: Donations from sailors covered all the costs
options.rationale: Voluntary giving is exactly what free riding undermines.

options.label: Ships paid nothing, because lighthouses ran on volunteers
options.rationale: Coase found private operators collecting dues.

questions.explanation: Passing ships had to dock somewhere, and the dues were collected there. Critics add that a royal patent backed the charge.
